MarBlue Atlas (new) for Kindle Case, Black (Fits Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle and Kindle Touch) This is a review of both the black and blue MarBlue Atlas Kindle Cases. These are decent cases and have some good things going for them. I wouldn't say they're great cases but they do the job with, what I consider, only a few flaws.

The system for attaching your Kindle to the cover are four very strong and quite tight rubber reinforced elastic cords. I've had several Kindles and numerous cases over the years and as far as four corner case mounts this is the most secure of that style I've ever seen. I had my PaperWhite mounted in this case and shook it violently, over a pillow and ready to catch it should anything happen, and not only did it stay in place it didn't move a fraction of an inch. I was very impressed with that function of the case.

The case exterior is a synthetic leather that truly looks and feels like leather. It is well made, and fairly handsome. Unlike many synthetic products this had no harsh chemical smell. The blue cover looks a little less like leather than the black but it is a very nice shade of blue.

The interior is an attractive, and soft, dark grey microfiber that's quite pleasing to the touch.

The case is held closed or open with a half inch wide cloth elastic that is well attached to the case. This holds the case closed quite well. The hinge area of the case is a bit too large/tall/wide making the case when folded back a little ungainly and if not strapped down it wanted to flop closed.

Inside the case is a nearly three inch wide strap made of the same soft, grey microfiber attached with elastics at both the top and bottom. This comes into use when the case is open you can put your hand or fingers under this strap to read one handed. With my PaperWhite I found this to be slightly uncomfortable making me arch my hand in an odd manner to get my thumb onto the screen. I'm not a fan of the strap, the sections at the top and bottom where it's stitched to the elastic create two lumps that sit directly on the Kindle's screen. They're soft but it's two unnecessary pressure points.

This case does not have the magnet that the Amazon brand case does that turns the kindle on and off when you open it. The power button on my PaperWhite was a little hard to reach with the shape of the case and the location of the mounting strap. It wasn't too difficult to use but it's nowhere near as easy as opening the case and having your Kindle come on.

In conclusion...
The case is decent. It's a little... gappy, the front cover bends when you have your hand in the strap and this creates a gap that will let debris into the case and onto your Kindle. I'm not crazy about the strap but that's more personal preference than anything else. This is a well made decently protective Kindle case.
text_fidelity_b: MarBlue Atlas (new) for Kindle Case, Black (Fits Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle and Kindle Touch)

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 (10.1-Inch, Wi-Fi) 2012 Model I thought long and hard about a tablet, knowing that for me it would basically be a toy. Plus I already had a Nook Color. When the iPad2 reduced in price, I thought about getting one of those, but decided against it for the following reasons: (1) no Flash--and yes, I know HTML5 is going to make that obsolete, but in the meantime many websites have a lot of money invested in Flash animation and even restaurants use the silly format to show you their menus (geez, just give us a LIST already--I don't need pretty pictures to find out if you serve something I can eat) and (2) I'm already invested in the Android market and would have to buy many iPad apps that I already have free from Android.

I have not even used it for a week yet, but this a preliminary review with some information I saw requested in other reviews (not necessarily here at Amazon).

UPS delivered this a little before 6:30 p.m. I immediately plugged it into the charger and left it alone. It was charged by 10 p.m. (it might have been earlier, but the unit was away from me and I heard no bleep or flash that might have have indicated the charge was finished). So it does not take six or eight or ten hours to charge as I have seen claimed on other sites. By midnight I was attached to wireless, had gotten into all my accounts and Android apps and was happily surfing and rearranging my home screen.

I used this over the weekend at a science fiction convention. I did not use it constantly, but turned the screen on and off all day for about a 12-hour period, reading Facebook and blogs, checking the news and weather, looking at the convention schedule online, playing short You Tube videos, etc. Nothing excessive, but sometimes did have it on for a half hour to 45-minutes at the time. I also do not have a lot of widgets going, like the Accu-Weather and news widgets that come pre-loaded on the home screen. (They delete easily.) In that 12-hour period it never got below 78% on the battery. It's very quick and fast and responds to a Targus stylus (rubber tipped) wonderfully, much better than my Nook color. The resolution of the screen is impressive. Maybe it's not the new iPad's "retinal display," but it's very, very sharp and bright, even though I keep my brightness turned down to save power. I downloaded the Nook app and the magazines I subscribe to look gorgeous and are simple to read; if not, a tap of the screen makes the text bigger. The unit also comes with Zinio preloaded, an app I plan to use to subscribe to non-US magazines. Kindle books look nice as well, but to me this is too large for marathon reading sessions. I prefer my Nook Color for that. Like my Android phone and my Nook Color, it connects to wireless like a dream, which is more than I can say for my laptop.

Things that might lead you to choose another tablet: (1) The camera is nothing special. It takes good close ups, but further away was problematic. However, I was in a low-light situation each time. Taking photos outside may be totally different. Why Samsung chose to remove the flash I have no idea. Silly, really. But who buys a tablet to take pictures with? (2) With a stylus I can tap to enlarge an image (like Google Maps), but not make it smaller and there is no plus or minus sign on the screen as on my Android phone. (3) Blogger doesn't work in the browser; you have to download the Blogger app, but that works well. iExit doesn't work on it, either. Rats. (4) As at least one other person mentioned, the screen cap button is right in a place where you can hit it easily. I thought of a good use for it this weekend (took a screen cap of the online schedule for the convention I was at, made a short-cut of it to the screen, then pulled up the screen cap for reference rather than going to the web page all the time). Very convenient! (5) Hate the pre-loaded websites in the browser, but I have seen this on other tablets. Apparently we the public are stupid (or lazy) and can't find our own favorite websites and bookmark them. [eyes roll], and (6) my Bluetooth keyboard won't work with it right now because there is as yet no driver for Android 4.0 (Ice Cream Sandwich).

I hope to check back with further comments.

[A few weeks later after I bought this, my husband found an Asus Transformer (TF300) at a good price. It appears to be just as good as this Samsung and the camera is better. It has a zoom and does take a better photo. So if you were looking for a tablet with a better camera the Asus Transformer may be for you. Note: It doesn't have a flash either.]

[Update July 31, 2012 to answer "How long does the battery last"?: I was sick and tired of not seeing any Olympic equestrian coverage except for a couple of hours in the wee hours of the morning, so downloaded the "Live Extra" Olympics app from the Android Market. This carries live streaming of events as well as archived events. This morning I watched about two hours of live streaming of the jumping finals. When that ended I watched six hours of cross-country eventing replay. Then about an hour and forty minutes of the replay of the jumping. I had my brightness at about 35%. This got me down to 10% of the battery from a full charge. Quite satisfactory.]
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 (10.1-Inch, Wi-Fi) 2012 Model

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Wireless Rechargeable Laser Mouse 7000 Mac/Windows I have mixed feelings about this mouse. On one hand it is a pleasure to use. On the other, charging it leaves much to be desired.

This is a fairly large mouse, sculpted nicely to fit most peoples' hands. I have large hands and I have found this mouse to be a good fit. It is comfortable to grip, the scroll wheel is smooth and easy to turn, and the buttons are easy to press without being hyper-sensitive. Ergonomics are this mouse's strongest attribute.

In use, the mouse is on par with other Microsoft mice I have used. It is accurate. Unlike some of the comments by other reviewers here, I have had no issue with it being too sensitive or too precise. The performance has, in my opinion, been average. This is not a bad thing - Microsoft mice are usually very consistent and this one fits the norm.

Where I ran into difficulty with this mouse was in charging it. I read a lot of other reviews on this mouse beforehand so I was prepared for issues with charging. That said, I was still having issues getting the mouse to charge the battery until I cut part of a 3x5 index card, folded it up and crammed it into the battery compartment with the battery. There have been enough other people that have had to do similarly odd things to rule out the possibility of this being an isolated case.

The battery can be put into a normal charger, but that defeats the purpose.

This is not a bad mouse. It's actually quite good and I would recommend it except for the recharging issue. As a wireless mouse it is fine, but as a recharging mouse it needs a design revisit.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Wireless Rechargeable Laser Mouse 7000 Mac/Windows

It's taken a real beating - dropped it several times, gets wet in the rain/snow, and so on. But, it just keeps on working! Got to love a product that can take a punch.

Reception is pretty good - can pick up several stations quite clearly, and a few more with some static. Sound quality is decent. You won't mistake it for CD-quality, but it's radio, after all. Battery life is very good - goes a few months on an AAA. I just switched to rechargeable batteries, but even with regular alkalines it's pretty cost effective.

The only downside I've encountered was the headphones. Found them to be very uncomfortable, and replaced them very soon after purchasing with a set of ear buds (not sure of the brand - perhaps Sony as well).

It's not as flexible as a MP3 player but I find the radio reception on this to be far better than the reception on my MP3 player that has an FM tuner. Yes, a conventional FM radio is a bit dated, but then again, so am I - sometimes it's nice to just listen to the radio. For the price, this is a great performer.

text_fidelity_a:
Sennheiser PXC 450 Active Noise-Canceling Headphones I spend a great deal of time in a computer lab where there is literally over 1,000 running systems. In this environment, ear protection isn't absolutely necessary but without it there's some discomfort with which to deal because of all the fans in these systems and the requisite air handling units. I already have a pair of Bose QC-15 headphones but I am not a huge fan, so I recently purchased a pair of Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones for use in this environment. After an initial break-in period, I have come to really appreciate them.

This is going to be a comparative review, though primarily about the Sennheiser phones. Bose is generally regarded as the gold standard when it comes to ANC headphones, so matching the Sennheisers to the Bose is a good match-up. I'll break it all down into categories: Noise Canceling, Comfort, Sound Quality and Build Quality.

Noise Canceling:
Active noise canceling is THE primary feature of these phones and each has its strengths. Bose is, without question, the more capable ANC set when it comes to removing noise. This supremacy comes at a price though - because of the aggressiveness of their ANC, the wearer often feels a "pressure" on the ears when using the phones, something not present with the Sennheiser set which is close to Bose's level of canceling. Where Bose went to extremes to eliminate noise, Sennheiser went with the thought of "good enough for most". To be sure, both sets do a nice job of eliminating low frequency noise, enough to make air travel more pleasant if you dislike the rumble of plane engines.

They work in the car too (if you're not driving). I tried both sets in a moving vehicle and all do a fine job of eliminating road and engine noise. In fact, it was quiet to the point of eerie in the car. So, if you're a passenger on a long trip, either of these will work to suit your needs.

For the Sennheisers, you don't have to use ANC to listen to music as they provide the ability to override ANC and work like normal headphones. Bose, on the other hand, is an all-or-nothing deal and requires ANC to be on when listening to anything at all.

And that brings up a nice little feature on the Sennheisers - the "talk-thru" function, which allows a listener to cut off all sound and turn on a small microphone so that one can carry on a conversation without having to remove the headphones. No other headset I have ever used has this feature and it has already proven to be a handy tool.

Both sets require a single AAA battery to provide ANC. The battery life is definitely better with the Bose - mine last about a week between needing new batteries, whereas the Sennheiser set needs a new battery every other day.

Comfort:
The Sennheisers are the most comfortable headphones I have ever worn - period. The padding is buttery soft and they fit over my ears with no issue. Other reviewers have said that it seems like they just melt into your head, and that's a very accurate way to describe them. The Bose are nearly as comfortable, though they are slightly smaller.

Where the Sennheisers have a slight comfort disadvantage is actually in their size. These are big headphones and when they are worn around the neck instead of on the ears, they tend to rub on the neck and sometimes (depending on what you're doing) they can get in the way. If you take them off, or don't wear them around your neck, there's nothing about which to complain.

Sound Quality:
Sennheiser has always had premium sound, and the PXC-450 headphones demonstrate why they are the champs when it comes to quality sound. Though not audiophile phones, the PXC-450 brings awesome sound quality even at low volumes, with very full midrange and decent bass. The Bose sound great, except that the bass is too rich and without an equalizer in the mix the bass is enough to give me a headache over extended periods.

Build Quality:
I have not had the Sennheiser set very long but so far I have had no trouble with them. They feel rugged and sturdy, though they are mostly plastic so they do scratch and twist easily. The cord is heavy gauge wire, a welcome improvement over the cabling on Sennheiser sets I have worn in the past. The Bose set is a little more flimsy, with lesser gauge wire.

In summary, I find that the Sennheiser PXC-450 headphones are a better product than the Bose QC-15 headphones. They sound great, feel comfortable and they do a fine job of canceling noise. Bose does have better ANC and if that is the main thing you need and you don't mind the sensation of pressure they put on the ears then Bose is a better choice, but in almost every other aspect the Sennheisers bring more to the table.
text_fidelity_b: Sennheiser PXC 450 Active Noise-Canceling Headphones

Logitech Z623 400 Watt Home Speaker System, 2.1 Speaker System - Black Latest edit after some frustrating months of use.

I ordered this as a TV speaker. That was in the description.
With no remote, and no way to raise or lower the sound without getting up, the item is useless to me. I like to watch TV in bed.
Who wants to keep getting up. As a computer speaker, it takes up a lot of space.very dissapointed.
I will donate it a church, where they will appreciate a loud speaker for youth groups.

Edit after 5 days use.

There is no remote. The volume is controlled by a dial. When using this connected to your TV, it's a major disadvantage getting up every time you need to change the volume. I have to downgrade from 5 stars to 4, because of this. They need to add to either a remote, or an app letting your phone control the volume. Not a problem when using this as a computer speaker, since the control is by your hand, not across the room. This is promoted as a TV speaker, not just a computer speaker, so it's a major fault.

Original review below.

I have been using the Logitech Z2300 that I purchased years ago. Connected to my computer and much appreciated when I listen to my apple subscription music. A real monster for a computer speaker. Thankfully, the Z 625 is decidedly smaller and fits on the bottom shelf of my 42 inch wood TV table with room to spare. There is also room left for my Amazon Echo and Braven wireless bluetooth speakers. The smaller size results in a much cleaner, more attractive package.

The dialog is much clearer than I expected. I have a ZVOX 450 on my main TV, so I do appreciate clear dialog.
I was disappointed that there is no bluetooth. The computer and Man Cave TV are on opposite sides of the same room, and having the Z2300 for music, and the Z625 for the TV is a bit too much. However, the problem was easily solved. On the Z625, I'm using the optical cable for the TV sound, and am using the enclosed jack to connect the speaker to my extra Iphone. As I type, I'm listening to Herman's Hermits through my Iphone to Z625 jack connection. The music is very soothing and suits my needs perfectly. No adjustments are needed when switching from the music through my smartphone via jack, or the TV sound through the optical cable. Automatic switching,

My TV test via optical was the opening of Game of Thrones. The subwoofer bass sounded great and added greatly to the enjoyment of watching the series. The galloping horses sounded thunderous.

Other considerations. I gave away my monstrous Polk system when we moved to our condo. Soundbars provide the cleanest look but really don't have any bass. My wife is picky. The soundbar is on the main TV for a cleaner appearance, while the Man Cave is a perfect home for this unit.

There was absolutely no documentation/instructions in the box, other than safety information. However hookup instructions were printed on the cardboard box. Don't destroy them opening it. Hooking up via optical was very intuitive and took minutes. I'd still like some instructions. For example, the power button is a push button. Does it shut off after inactivity? I'm doing it manually. Going by the Z2300, it probably won't make any difference. These are built to last.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Z623 400 Watt Home Speaker System, 2.1 Speaker System - Black

Accepts grounded plugs, but will not transfer ground. Be aware of this. It does have a dummy ground on the UK/mid-East plug to defeat stupid tamper resistant outlets.

No Italy plug. None of them have this. Italy loves to be a pain. Can force a schuko plug in sometimes.

US and Australia/NZ plugs are different. This part I like better than how some of the others use one set of adjustable prongs.

I only use these when traveling to multiple regions at once or when I might need multiple USB ports simultaneously. They are cool, but still a bit large.

There are some differences between different models, and I like the US/NZ plugs are different, but it's hard to justify not getting one with a USB-C port with higher amperage out at this point in time.

Compared to the EA2700 which this router is replacing, the download speed is noticeably faster. The router is easy to install, fairly intuitve design for the app (though I really don't much use for it - it may be of value if you anticipate multiple devices streaming media content simultaneously and need to prioritize a security cam or work laptop over other connections. The 2 USB storage and 4 gigabit ethernet ports, the dual-band, and ease of set-up makes this a very compelling choice. I can go days before even thinking of needing to charge. My only main beef with the Fire tablets... is it's an Amazon product so they want you to use their app store. Which is as sparse as the Windows store. I know there are ways to get the Google Play store on it, but for the average buyer that seems like an unnecessary hassle. And it is. I didn't buy this tablet to download a bunch of apps. I bought it to watch movies and videos and browse the internet when I was at work or away from my computer and didn't want to drain my phone battery. So for me it's fine. TV Antenna, Digital TV Antenna for Smart TV Indoor, Strong Magnetic Base for Easy Installation, 360°& Long Range Reception for HDTV Channels-Support All Tv's-10ft Long Cables Our house is about 40 miles east of the local CBS and FOX affiliate's transmitter, and maybe 10 miles the same direction from the others. The TV is beside an east wall with large front windows. We had been using one of the flat amplified antennas, and it just couldn't get the distant station. I don't know if the signals didn't want to go through too many walls, or if the high voltage electric transmission line running along the east edge of our front yard was responsible.

When I installed this antenna, I still couldn't get CBS. With the nice long piece of coax attached to it, I experimented with various places. The window was a no go, no matter where it was placed, giving my power line hypothesis some points. Holding it high its full distance to the west worked. We are lucky enough to have a tall bookshelf there, so I stuck it to a metal bookend on top of it. Success!

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) When my husband recently purchased a [[ASIN:B0071N6AC6 netbook]], he wasn't using his Kindle Fire nearly as much, and I inherited it. I had recently dumped my cable TV service in favor of using the Fire to watch online the few news and TV dramas that I normally had used my TiVo to record. I found that my Internet connection through a wifi router has a really hard time playing videos via the Fire. It would often lose connectivity or freeze up when my iPhone was working fine using the same connection, playing the same shows.

The Fire has a gorgeous interface, though, for reading eBooks compared to my Kindle Keyboard. However, I've been using a Kindle app so frequently the past few months on my iPhone, that both the Kindle Keyboard and the Kindle Fire feel too cumbersome to bother with most of the time in comparison as an eReader.

For searching the Internet, the Fire has an easier interface than the iPhone, so I use it more often for that, unless I don't have it with me--I always have my iPhone with me.

I don't use the Fire for MP3. It is just too huge compared to my tiny MP3 player.

I don't have magazine subscriptions in electronic form, so I don't use it for that, though I know I could if I wanted to.

I understand the Fire can support PDF, but I haven't used it for that yet.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)
